Two things here:

**Images vs Text:** Go with **Images**. The screenshots showing your onboarding flow (genre picker, budget selector) give users a feel for the app before tapping. Text ads only show a description snippet and are much easier to scroll past. Image ads have higher tap-through rates for apps with visual UI.

**"There is no free plan" text:** That description in the text ad is being pulled from your **App Store product page description or promotional text**. Apple Search Ads uses your Default Product Page copy. You likely have that phrase somewhere in your App Store Connect description/subtitle/promotional text.

Let me check your app metadata to find where it's coming from.

That text isn't in your codebase - it's coming from your **App Store Connect listing**. The "There is no free plan! You must pay to use this!" line is in your app's description on App Store Connect, and Apple Search Ads pulls that as the text ad snippet.

**Action items:**

1. **Go with Images** for your search ads - they showcase the app much better
2. **Update your App Store Connect description** - the current opening line is actively discouraging downloads. Instead of leading with "There is no free plan!", lead with the value proposition. Something like: *"AI-powered vinyl record identification & pricing for collectors, dealers, and music lovers"* - then mention the subscription details further down in the description.

Even if you run image ads, that description still shows on your product page and can hurt conversion. The first line matters most since it's what appears before "more..."

how do i make a custom product page in app store connect

Select **Default** instead - you don't need a custom product page right now.

Custom product pages are for A/B testing different screenshots/descriptions for different audiences. That's an optimization for later once you have data on what converts.

For now, **Default** will use your existing App Store listing which is fine to start. Just make sure you update that description first (remove the "no free plan" line) before the ads go live.

Once you're getting consistent installs and want to test different creatives, then you can create custom product pages in App Store Connect under **App Store > Custom Product Pages**.

Here's the reality:

**Your current setup:** Pure StoreKit 2 with 4 custom-built SwiftUI paywall screens (PricingView, PromoOfferView, FreeTrialPromoView, SpecialOfferView) - ~1,500 lines of paywall UI code plus ~500 lines of subscription management.

**What Superwall integration would involve:**
1. Add Superwall SDK (SPM or CocoaPods)
2. Recreate all 4 paywall screens in Superwall's dashboard or configure them to wrap your existing views
3. Replace all paywall presentation logic with Superwall's triggers
4. Wire up StoreKit purchases through Superwall's purchase handler
5. Migrate your trial logic, spin wheel flow, and special offer routing
6. Test all flows end-to-end

**Honest assessment:** Your paywall system is heavily custom (spin wheel, promo flows, trial gating, free scan limits). This isn't a simple drop-in. You're looking at a solid effort to migrate without breaking things.

**My recommendation:** Don't do it yet. Superwall shines when you want to A/B test different paywall designs remotely. You haven't even run ads yet - you don't have conversion data to optimize against. Get your ads running, collect data for 2-4 weeks, then decide if paywall optimization is your bottleneck. If your install-to-trial rate is low, *then* Superwall makes sense.
there's no way to straight up add the code into superwall?

You can't paste your SwiftUI views into Superwall directly. Superwall paywalls are either built in their dashboard editor or using their no-code templates.

**Your two options with Superwall:**

1. **Rebuild your paywalls in Superwall's dashboard** - Use their visual editor to recreate how your screens look. This is the standard approach but means rebuilding 4 screens from scratch in their tool.

2. **Use Superwall as a wrapper** - Keep your existing SwiftUI views but use Superwall to control *when* they show up (triggers, rules, A/B testing). You'd register your views with Superwall's `PaywallPresentationHandler`. This is less work but you lose the remote editing benefit.

Either way it's not a copy-paste. But option 2 is much faster since you keep your existing code and just add Superwall's triggering layer on top.

Again though - I'd focus on getting your ads live and fixing that App Store description first. Those will move the needle more than changing your paywall infrastructure right now.

[Image: original 2216x1400, displayed at 2000x1264. Multiply coordinates by 1.11 to map to original image.]

Your app isn't showing up because Superwall pulls from the App Store search index - newer/smaller apps sometimes don't appear. Try selecting **"Not released yet?"** at the top and enter your Bundle ID manually (`com.vinylscout` or whatever it is in your Xcode project). That should work.

**Alternatives for A/B testing paywalls:**

1. **Apple's native A/B testing** - Yes, App Store Connect has **Product Page Optimization** built in. You can test up to 3 treatment variations of your screenshots, app icon, and preview videos. It's free and built into App Store Connect under your app's page. However, it only tests the *product page*, not in-app paywalls.

2. **Remote config your own A/B test** - You could use Firebase Remote Config (free) to serve different paywall variants to different users and track conversion yourself through PostHog. This is more work but no SDK dependency.

3. **RevenueCat Paywalls** - RevenueCat has a paywall builder with A/B testing and it integrates with StoreKit 2. Free tier available. More focused on payments than Superwall.

**My take:** Try the "Not released yet?" option on Superwall with your bundle ID first. If that doesn't work, honestly just use Firebase Remote Config + PostHog to A/B test. You already have PostHog set up, and a simple boolean flag to show paywall A vs B is like 20 lines of code.
